description: This team consists of 4 members from Charlotte, North Carolina.
summary: We created HALO (Health App for Long-Duration Operations) for astronauts to keep track of their health and know what to do during spaceflight. The stand-out part of HALO is an interactive 3D human body which has skeleton and muscle layers. It includes body systems that are color coded red, green, yellow, and communicate what needs to be addressed. Clicking on different body systems allows the user to learn about what it does, how spaceflight affects it, and what the best course of actions are to take based on user data. The system allows the user to toggle different locations, and this automatically adjusts for health risks, radiation limits, and emergency protocols for that specific environment. Our app constantly compares the astronauts daily vitals, sleep, and mood against their own personal baseline, and explains every alert that occurs. It also includes an emergency feature to guide the crew in the event of an emergency in which communication from Earth will take too long. It helps guide the crew through CPR, bleeding, and breathing problems. The app is powered by data from NASA; it includes astronaut blood samples from the Inspirit4 mission and live space-weather alerts from NASA’s DONKI system.
details:
HALO is a web app that lets astronauts check their own health based on several metrics. In the main screen is an interactive 3D human body with skin, muscle and skeleton, heart and blood vessels, and organ layers. Clicking a system shows what it does, how spaceflight affects it, what to do now, and when to get help. In the daily check-in, astronauts log vitals such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen and temperature, along with sleep, mood and symptoms. Each astronaut is compared to the baseline for each health metric, which they can track with detailed graphs. 

On space missions to different planets, the space crew will be too far from Earth for quick communication. On Mars, a message can take up to about 20 minutes to reach Earth, so astronauts won’t be able to contact any doctor on Earth with speed. HALO guides the crew on handling their own medical care, which matches NASA’s goal of Earth-independent medical operations.

We built HALO in TypeScript using React and Vite, with Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion for the interface and Recharts for trend charts. The 3D body uses Three.js through React Three Fiber, with open source anatomy models. We also utilized the Web Speech API to read questions aloud and listen for answers. We used Python scripts to download NASA data including: Inspiration4 crew blood counts from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569), and space-weather events from NASA’s DONKI API, including solar particle events and geomagnetic storms. The AI assistant uses the Claude API running Haiku 5.5. The app is hosted on Vercel and only requires a laptop or tablet with a camera and microphone.

Within HALO, there are several environments that have different priorities, which includes the ISS, Mars transit, a lunar base, a rover, and a Mars base. Gravity, radiation levels, health priorities and how to get help are all different based on the astronauts’ environment. On the ISS, the astronauts have the ability to reach a flight surgeon, whereas on Mars, messages are queued with a countdown for when a reply can arrive. 

HALO can also use a camera as a tool for pulse readings, skin photo comparisons, and a vision grid test for eye changes. The buddy check lets crewmates rate how each other seem, since people often notice tiredness or withdrawal in a teammate before that person does. 

Astronauts may have trouble meeting their daily medical needs, so we added a gamified routine to motivate astronauts to complete tasks. Everything is attributed with markers like color or shape for increased readability. Also, based on our research, astronauts sometimes underreport symptoms to avoid being grounded, so the journal is private. 

In the future, something we’d like to implement is to offload all of the non-local features of the app into a completely local-run software that only runs on the hardware it is being utilized on. For example, for our AI chatbot, we are using the Claude API, which accesses servers across Earth, which is a parameter that hinders fast communication from far in outer space. By converting this into a local model, the astronauts will only need the device they are using to be able to use every feature within HALO.
